title: Leaders Who Make Relationships a Task to Achieve
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Describes task-focused leaders who, upon hearing their relationships are frayed, respond by treating relationship-building itself as a task -- a round of individual lunches, then back to focus on execution. Argues this approach fails because it treats people as a problem to solve rather than an investment worth understanding, so the gesture is perceived as a ploy rather than genuine care. The piece's underlying claim is that extreme task focus creates a gap between how a leader feels about people and how those people actually feel treated, and that closing this gap requires expanding what counts as effectiveness beyond task completion alone.
points: Task-focused leaders who treat relationship repair as another task to complete (a round of lunches) typically make things worse, not better.
People don't feel respected or cared for when a leader approaches them as a problem to solve rather than a relationship to invest in.
The real fix requires task-focused leaders to expand what counts as effectiveness, closing the gap between how they feel about people and how they make people feel.
quotes: A leader who is extremely task-focused is told that their relationships are becoming frayed. So, instead of working on the relationships, they make them a task.
Unfortunately, the more task-focused they become, the more likely it is for them to undermine their relationships with the people who help them execute.
Their drive, urgency, and relentless pursuit of outcomes typically make them insensitive to the needs and concerns of others.
The problem is that relationships that get treated as outcomes to achieve and tasks to complete never fully form or develop.
People don’t feel respected, important, or cared for when a leader sees them as a problem to solve. The lunch (and anything like it) is seen as a ploy, not as an investment in time and understanding.
It’s usually not because they don’t care about people. But their extreme task focus creates a huge gap between how they feel about people and how they make people feel.
